metadata.title: Claude Code, Plugin Settings.
metadata.purpose: Take apart the plugin-settings case: explain why Claude Code re-reads state from a file every session instead of remembering it, evaluate the .claude/plugin-name.local.md split — YAML frontmatter for machines, markdown body for humans — and name the trade the sed-based hook makes: cheap and reliable on flat fields, silently wrong on structured YAML. Land the carry-out that a settings file is read fresh every time, in a shape simple enough for the parser you shipped.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the enabled field driving the quick-exit pattern: toggles reliably when flat, silently mis-parsed when the YAML gets complex)

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening. Claude Code boots blank between sessions on purpose — no hidden memory to lean on. So the real question isn't remembering. It's parsing: what does it read, and how?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How do I get Claude Code to remember my plugin's settings between sessions?', hesitates on 'remember', corrects to 'read', lands the real question

props.text:
How do I get Claude Code
to remember my plugin's
settings between sessions?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('remember' -> 'read') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Ask Claude in chat to remember a setting and it evaporates the moment the process ends — chat memory lives inside one conversation, nowhere else. What survives is a file on disk: dot-claude slash plugin-name dot local dot md, in the project root. They split it deliberately. Above a divider, YAML frontmatter — flat key-value fields, enabled, mode, a retry count, the sort of thing a script can grep. Below, a markdown body for the free-form prose a human reads. One file, two audiences.

shot.new_visual_element: A conversation bubble scattering past a session-restart divider; beside it a file icon staying fixed; the file splits into a frontmatter block on top and a markdown body block below

production_viz.label: A file, not a memory
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a speech-bubble labelled 'remember' fades and scatters as a vertical divider line labelled 'new session' sweeps past it. Right: a file icon labelled '.local.md' stays fixed and solid through the same divider, unaffected. The file then splits horizontally: the top region fills with flat key: value lines labelled 'YAML frontmatter'; the bottom region fills with wrapped prose lines labelled 'markdown body'.

beats.narration_text: Three consumers, one file, three different machineries. The hook is a bash script — parses the frontmatter with sed, no Claude in the loop at all. A slash command uses the Read tool, inside Claude's own context. An agent references the file directly in its instructions. Here's the anchor: one field, enabled, drives a quick-exit pattern — check the file exists, check enabled, and if it's false, exit zero before doing anything else.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — three consumer icons pointing at one file, then enabled: true/false driving a hook through check-file, check-enabled, to run or exit 0

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — one field, quick exit
production_viz.mechanic: Three cards fade in around a central file icon: 'hook' (terminal glyph, 'bash, parses with sed'), 'command' (magnifying glass, 'Read tool'), 'agent' (a simple figure glyph, 'in its instructions') — each with an arrow into the file. THE ANCHOR. Cards fade; below, a file corner reading 'enabled: true' zooms in, feeding a check-sequence box: 'file exists?' -> 'enabled?' -> branching to 'run' (teal) or 'exit 0' (terracotta). Toggle the field to false: the path lights straight to exit 0. THIS EXACT SEQUENCE RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Flip enabled again — false, true, false — and the hook obeys every time. That's sed doing what it was built for: line-shaped input, a flat boolean, one match per line. But hand it structure — a multiline value, a quoted colon, an indented block — and the same parser silently mangles it. No error, no exit code, no complaint. The frontmatter just stops matching what's on the page. That's the trade the design made: a two-line bash extraction on one side, no real YAML understanding on the other. This works if you keep the schema flat; it fails the moment you don't.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — enabled toggling the hook correctly three times, then a complex YAML block passing through the same sed scan and coming out wrong, no error shown

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — reliable, then silently wrong
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CHECK SEQUENCE RETURNS, identical, and answers correctly three times in a row as 'enabled' flips false/true/false — each marked teal 'correct'. Then a second frontmatter block appears, this one with a quoted, colon-bearing value and an indented sub-list. A magnifying glass sweeps across it line by line, mimicking sed; when it crosses the quoted colon and the indented block, the extracted value shown beside it visibly does not match the source text, and a small label reads 'no error — just wrong'.

beats.narration_text: A plugin's settings aren't something you ask Claude to remember. They're a file it reads back every time, in a shape simple enough for the parser you shipped — or not parsed at all.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm building a Claude Code plugin and I need persistent settings that survive between sessions — because Claude itself won't carry state, the settings have to live in a file the plugin reads back every time. Design the whole scheme. The exact file path, and why it should live in the project's dot-claude directory rather than the user's home. What belongs in YAML frontmatter — the machine-facing structured fields — versus a markdown body for the human-facing prose. A bash hook that parses the frontmatter with sed and quick-exits before doing anything if an enabled field is false or missing, showing me the actual code. And the three shapes of YAML value that will silently mis-parse with a sed-based extractor, plus what to do about them — reach for a real YAML parser like yq, or forbid those shapes in the schema. Go deeper: ask the same model what happens when two plugins on the same machine both want a settings file. Do they collide in dot-claude, or does each get its own sub-namespace? And what does it cost you if a stale settings file from an uninstalled plugin gets read anyway?
